title: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface takes the shortest path: \kappa_g = 0

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter X, “A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics”; topic “Muscle fibres of hollow organs”. Scope: muscular walls of hollow and tubular organs (heart, stomach, blood vessels, gut, worm body wall)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface takes the shortest path: \kappa_g = 0

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch10-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fibre geometry is measurable in modern 3D datasets, and representative organs can be analyzed quickly. The causal 'automatically' mechanism and broad organ scope remain confounded by development and function.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map muscle-fibre trajectories onto 3D organ surfaces and compute geodesic curvature and path length relative to endpoint-matched shortest paths. Developmental or mechanical data must additionally test whether tension causes alignment rather than merely correlating with it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Geodesic alignment does not prove automatic tension-driven arrangement.

Anatomical fibre tracts often have changing insertion points and layered helices.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shortest paths on a measured surface are a clear test, and public cardiac diffusion data plus ventricular shape models make the heart part feasible with specialist but existing tools. The claim names a list of hollow organs for which comparable open fiber maps are sparse. A heart-only result would resolve a restricted scope and leave the general automatic-arrangement claim open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On reconstructed surfaces of heart, stomach, arteries and gut, compare muscle-fiber trajectories with computed geodesics. Fibers lying on shortest paths, annular and longitudinal on a simple tube, support the claim; systematic extra length or a non-geodesic helix would refute it for that organ.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Myocardial fibers also follow sheet architecture and load, so a geodesic fit can be confounded with stress alignment.

Open fiber-orientation data are concentrated on the human left ventricle, not the stomach, arteries, intestine or worm body wall.
